verses.1:1: May he kiss me with a kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine,
verses.1:2: fragrant with the finest ointments. Oil poured out is your name; therefore young women have loved you.
verses.1:3: Draw me; we will run after you toward the fragrance of your ointments. The king has brought me into his storerooms; we will exult and be glad in you, remembering your breasts more than wine. The upright love you.
verses.1:4: I am black, yet lovely, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.
verses.1:5: Do not stare at me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me. My mother's sons fought against me; they placed me as keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.
verses.1:6: Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday, so that I may not begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.
verses.1:7: If you do not know yourself, most beautiful among women, go out, and go after the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your young goats beside the tents of the shepherds.
verses.1:8: To my cavalry in the chariots of Pharaoh I have compared you, my friend.
verses.1:9: Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove; your neck is like necklaces.
verses.1:10: We will make little gold chains for you, inlaid with silver.
verses.1:11: While the king was at his couch, my spikenard gave off its fragrance.
verses.1:12: A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; between my breasts he will stay.
verses.1:13: A cluster of henna is my beloved to me in the vineyards of En-gedi.
verses.1:14: Look, you are beautiful, my friend! Look, you are beautiful! Your eyes are those of doves.
verses.1:15: Look, you are beautiful, my beloved, and charming! Our bed is in bloom.
verses.1:16: The beams of our houses are of cedar; our paneled ceilings are of cypress.
verses.2:1: I am a flower of the field, and a lily of the valleys.
verses.2:2: Like a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.
verses.2:3: Like an apple tree among the trees of the forests, so is my beloved among the sons. Beneath the shade of the one whom I had desired I sat down, and his fruit was sweet to my palate.
verses.2:4: He brought me into the wine cellar; he set love in order within me.
verses.2:5: Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I am faint with love.
verses.2:6: His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.
verses.2:7: I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roe deer and stags of the fields, neither to rouse nor to awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.
verses.2:8: The voice of my beloved! Look, here he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding across the hills.
verses.2:9: My beloved is like a roe deer and a fawn of the stags. See, he himself stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, peering through the lattices.
verses.2:10: Look, my beloved speaks to me: "Rise up, hurry, my friend, my dove, my lovely one, and come;
verses.2:11: for now winter has passed; the rain has departed and withdrawn.
verses.2:12: Flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has arrived; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land;
verses.2:13: the fig tree has put forth its unripe figs; the blossoming vineyards have given off their fragrance. Rise up, my friend, my exquisite one, and come,
verses.2:14: my dove, in the crevices of the rock, in the hollow of the wall, show me your face, let your voice sound in my ears; for your voice is sweet, and your face is charming."
verses.2:15: Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, for our vineyard has blossomed.
verses.2:16: My beloved belongs to me, and I to him, who feeds among the lilies,
verses.2:17: until the day breathes and the shadows decline. Return; my beloved, be like a roe deer and a fawn of the stags upon the mountains of Bether.
verses.3:1: On my bed, through the nights, I sought the one whom my soul loves; I sought him, and did not find him.
verses.3:2: "I will rise and go around the city; through the streets and squares I will seek the one whom my soul loves." I sought him, and did not find him.
verses.3:3: The watchmen who guard the city found me: "Have you seen the one whom my soul loves?"
verses.3:4: When I had passed just a little beyond them, I found the one whom my soul loves; I held him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother's house, and into the bedroom of the one who bore me.
verses.3:5: I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roe deer and stags of the fields, neither to rouse nor to awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.
verses.3:6: Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and of all the perfumer's powder?
verses.3:7: Look, sixty mighty men from the mightiest of Israel surround Solomon's bed,
verses.3:8: all holding swords, and most skilled for battles, each one's sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.
verses.3:9: King Solomon made a palanquin for himself from the timbers of Lebanon;
verses.3:10: he made its pillars of silver, its backrest of gold, its ascent of purple; its interior he lined with love, for the sake of the daughters of Jerusalem.
verses.3:11: Go out and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal, and on the day of the gladness of his heart.
verses.4:1: How beautiful you are, my friend! How beautiful you are! Your eyes are those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within. Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead.
verses.4:2: Your teeth are like flocks of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all with twin offspring, and there is no barren one among them.
verses.4:3: Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet. Like a piece of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, apart from what lies hidden within.
verses.4:4: Your neck is like the tower of David, which was built with battlements; a thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty.
verses.4:5: Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a roe deer, that feed among the lilies.
verses.4:6: Until the day breathes and the shadows decline, I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.
verses.4:7: You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no blemish in you.
verses.4:8: Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come, you will be crowned: from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the lairs of lions, from the mountains of leopards.
verses.4:9: You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of hair on your neck.
verses.4:10: How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! More beautiful than wine are your breasts, and the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.
verses.4:11: Your lips are a dripping honeycomb, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.
verses.4:12: An enclosed garden is my sister, my bride; an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain.
verses.4:13: Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates with the produce of fruit trees, henna with nard.
verses.4:14: Nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon; myrrh and aloe, with all the finest ointments.
verses.4:15: A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters that flow with force from Lebanon.
verses.4:16: Rise up, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow.
verses.5:1: Let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his fruit trees. I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have harvested my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, friends, and drink, and become drunk, dearest ones.
verses.5:2: I sleep, and my heart keeps watch. The voice of my beloved knocking: "Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my unblemished one, for my head is full of dew, and my curls with the drops of the nights."
verses.5:3: I have taken off my tunic; how will I put it on? I have washed my feet; how will I soil them?
verses.5:4: My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch.
verses.5:5: I rose to open to my beloved; my hands dripped myrrh, and my fingers were full of the purest myrrh.
verses.5:6: I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved, but he had turned aside and passed on. My soul melted when he spoke; I searched for him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me.
verses.5:7: The watchmen who go around the city found me; they struck me and wounded me. The watchmen of the walls took my cloak from me.
verses.5:8: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, tell him that I am faint with love.
verses.5:9: What is your beloved like compared to another beloved, most beautiful of women? What is your beloved like compared to another beloved, that you have adjured us like this?
verses.5:10: My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands.
verses.5:11: His head is the finest gold; his locks are like shoots of palm trees, black as a raven.
verses.5:12: His eyes are like doves by brooks of water, which have been washed with milk and sit beside the fullest streams.
verses.5:13: His cheeks are like beds of spices planted by perfumers. His lips are lilies, dripping the finest myrrh.
verses.5:14: His hands are rounded, golden, full of jacinths. His belly is ivory, studded with sapphires.
verses.5:15: His legs are marble pillars that are founded upon golden bases. His appearance is like that of Lebanon, choice as the cedars.
verses.5:16: His throat is most sweet, and he is wholly desirable. Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.
verses.5:17: Where has your beloved gone, most beautiful of women? Where has your beloved turned aside? And we will search for him with you.
verses.6:1: My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to feed in the gardens and gather lilies.
verses.6:2: I belong to my beloved, and my beloved belongs to me, he who feeds among the lilies.
verses.6:3: You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrifying as an army's battle line drawn up in order.
verses.6:4: Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away. Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead.
verses.6:5: Your teeth are like a flock of sheep that have come up from the washing, all with twin offspring, and there is no barren one among them.
verses.6:6: Like the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, apart from what is hidden in you.
verses.6:7: There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and of young women there is no number.
verses.6:8: My dove, my perfect one, is one alone; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her. The daughters saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; the queens and the concubines, and they praised her.
verses.6:9: Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, choice as the sun, terrifying as an army's battle line drawn up in order?
verses.6:10: I went down into the nut garden to see the fruits of the valleys, and to look whether the vine had blossomed and the pomegranates had budded.
verses.6:11: I did not know: my soul threw me into turmoil because of the chariots of Amminadab.
verses.6:12: Return, return, Shulammite! Return, return, so that we may gaze at you.
verses.7:1: What will you see in the Shulammite, except dances of camps? How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince! The joints of your thighs are like necklaces that have been fashioned by the hand of a craftsman.
verses.7:2: Your navel is a rounded bowl, never lacking drinks. Your belly is like a mound of wheat hedged around with lilies.
verses.7:3: Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a roe deer.
verses.7:4: Your neck is like an ivory tower; your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon that are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.
verses.7:5: Your head is like Carmel, and the locks of your head are like a king's purple bound in channels.
verses.7:6: How beautiful you are, and how lovely, dearest, in delights!
verses.7:7: Your stature is likened to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters.
verses.7:8: I said, "I will climb up into the palm tree and take hold of its fruits; and your breasts will be like clusters of the vine, and the fragrance of your mouth like that of apples."
verses.7:9: Your throat is like the finest wine, worthy for my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew over.
verses.7:10: I belong to my beloved, and toward me is his turning.
verses.7:11: Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field; let us stay in the villages.
verses.7:12: Early in the morning let us rise to go to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the blossoms are bringing forth fruits, whether the pomegranates have blossomed; there I will give you my breasts.
verses.7:13: The mandrakes have given forth fragrance; at our gates are all fruits: new and old, my beloved, I have saved for you.
verses.8:1: Who would give you to me as my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother, so that I might find you outside and kiss you, and now no one would despise me?
verses.8:2: I will take hold of you and lead you into the house of my mother; there you will teach me, and I will give you a cup of spiced wine and the new wine of my pomegranates.
verses.8:3: His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.
verses.8:4: I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, neither to rouse nor to awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.
verses.8:5: Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning on her beloved? Under the apple tree I roused you; there your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated.
verses.8:6: Place me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong like death, jealousy unyielding like the underworld; its torches are torches of fire and of flames.
verses.8:7: Many waters could not extinguish love, nor will rivers overwhelm it. If a man gives all the wealth of his house for love, he will despise it as nothing.
verses.8:8: Our sister is small, and she has no breasts; what will we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken to?
verses.8:9: If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon it; if she is a door, let us fasten it together with cedar planks.
verses.8:10: I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower, since I have become before him as one finding peace.
verses.8:11: The peaceful one had a vineyard in that which has peoples; he handed it over to keepers; a man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.
verses.8:12: My vineyard is before me. A thousand belong to you, the peaceful one, and two hundred to those who keep its fruits.
verses.8:13: You who live in the gardens, the friends are listening; let me hear your voice.
verses.8:14: Flee, my beloved, and be like a roe deer and a fawn of the stags upon the mountains of spices.

notes.1:1: The Vulgate reads ubera tua ("your breasts," here in native 1:1 and in native 1:3; Saints 1:2 and 1:4), following the Septuagint's reading of the unpointed Hebrew consonants rather than the Masoretic Text's "your love/caresses." Also, osculo ("a kiss") is singular in the Latin. Native Vulgate Song of Songs omits the title verse from numbering in ch. 1 (1:1-16 = Saints 1:2-17), places Saints 6:1 at 5:17, shifts 6:1-12 to Saints 6:2-7:1a, restores 7:1 (Saints 7:1b-2), and shifts 7:2-13 to Saints 7:3-14.
notes.1:3: The phrase in odorem unguentorum tuorum ("toward the fragrance of your ointments") follows the Septuagint and is absent from the Masoretic Text. In the closing sentence, the Vulgate renders Hebrew meysharim ("rightly/uprightly") as a plural noun, recti ("the upright").
notes.1:4: Latin pelles ("skins/hides," echoing the Septuagint) refers to leather tent-hangings, whereas the Hebrew has "curtains."
notes.1:7: The Vulgate follows the Septuagint with Si ignoras te ("If you do not know yourself"), whereas the Hebrew has an ethical dative meaning simply "If you do not know."
notes.1:9: Latin sicut turturis ("like those of a turtledove") reflects the Septuagint's reading of the Hebrew word tor as "turtledove" rather than "strings of ornaments."
notes.2:1: Latin flos campi ("a flower of the field") follows the Septuagint in translating Hebrew sharon as a common noun ("plain/field") rather than the proper place name "Sharon."
notes.2:4: The Vulgate's ordinavit in me caritatem ("he set love in order within me") follows the Septuagint's verbal reading of the Hebrew term that the Masoretic Text reads as a noun ("his banner over me was love").
notes.2:5: Latin floribus ("with flowers") is a Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew refers to "raisin cakes."
notes.2:7: Here (and in 3:5) the Vulgate renders the feminine noun concretely as dilectam ("the beloved"), referring to the bride rather than to abstract "love" as in the Hebrew.
notes.2:12: Latin tempus putationis ("the time of pruning") follows the Septuagint in taking the ambiguous Hebrew term zamir to mean vine-pruning rather than "singing."
notes.3:6: The Vulgate reads per desertum ("through the wilderness") and singular diminutive virgula fumi ("a slender column of smoke"), whereas the Hebrew has "from the wilderness" and plural "columns of smoke."
notes.3:7: Latin lectulum ("bed") repeats the same noun used in 1:16 and 3:1, whereas the Hebrew term here denotes a portable couch or litter.
notes.3:10: Latin ascensum ("ascent," following the Septuagint) corresponds to "seat" in the Hebrew, and propter filias Jerusalem ("for the sake of the daughters of Jerusalem") differs from the Hebrew "by the daughters of Jerusalem."
notes.4:1: Latin absque eo quod intrinsecus latet ("apart from what lies hidden within," repeated in 4:3; cf. absque occultis tuis in 6:7) is a distinctive Vulgate reading where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "behind your veil."
notes.4:8: Latin coronaberis ("you will be crowned") is a distinctive Vulgate reading where the Hebrew verb means "depart" or "look down."
notes.4:9: Latin vulnerasti ("you have wounded") and in uno crine colli tui ("with one lock of hair on your neck") preserve distinctive Vulgate readings where the Hebrew refers to captivating the heart with a single jewel of a necklace.
notes.4:10: Latin mammae and ubera ("breasts") and pulchriora ("more beautiful") follow the Septuagint tradition, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "love" (or "caresses") and "better."
notes.4:11: Latin thuris ("of frankincense") differs from the Masoretic Hebrew "of Lebanon"; conversely, in 4:14 the Vulgate reads lignis Libani ("trees of Lebanon") where the Hebrew reads "trees of frankincense."
notes.5:1: In the Clementine Vulgate, the opening sentence ("Let my beloved come...") begins chapter 5 rather than closing 4:16 as in the Hebrew text. At the end of the verse, carissimi ("dearest ones") reads the final word as a vocative rather than "with love."
notes.5:4: Latin ad tactum ejus ("at his touch") is a distinctive Vulgate reading where the Hebrew reads simply "for him."
notes.5:10: Latin electus ex millibus ("chosen from among thousands") has "thousands" rather than the Masoretic Hebrew "ten thousand."
notes.5:11: Latin elatae palmarum ("shoots of palm trees," from Greek elatai) refers to the budding spathes or shoots of date palms, where the Hebrew describes wavy locks or palm fronds.
notes.5:13: Latin consitae a pigmentariis ("planted by perfumers") is a distinctive Vulgate reading where the Hebrew reads "yielding fragrance" or "banks of spices."
notes.6:3: Latin suavis ("sweet") translates the Hebrew place name Tirzah etymologically according to its sense of "pleasant" or "delightful," following the Septuagint tradition.
notes.6:4: Latin quia ipsi me avolare fecerunt ("for they have made me fly away") follows the Septuagint's vivid rendering where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "for they overwhelm me."
notes.6:9: Latin electa ut sol ("choice as the sun") follows the Septuagint (eklekte) in taking the underlying Hebrew adjective in the sense of "select" rather than "bright."
notes.6:11: Latin conturbavit me ("threw me into turmoil") and the proper name Aminadab (standard modern English "Amminadab") preserve a distinctive Vulgate reading where the obscure Hebrew may be read "set me among the chariots of my noble people." In native Vulgate numbering this verse is 6:11 (Saints 6:12); native 6:12 ('Revertere, revertere, Sulamitis!...') ends chapter 6, and Hebrew 6:13b-7:1 corresponds to native Vulgate 7:1.
notes.6:12: Native Vulgate 6:12 ends chapter 6 ('Revertere, revertere, Sulamitis!...'; parallel to Saints 7:1a / Hebrew 6:13a), while restored native 7:1 opens chapter 7 with 'Quid videbis in Sulamite...'.
notes.7:1: Restored native Clementine Vulgate verse 7:1 (parallel to Hebrew 6:13b-7:1 / Saints 7:1b-2). Latin 'choros castrorum' literally means "dances [or companies] of camps" (rendering Hebrew Mahanaim), and 'Juncturæ femorum tuorum' literally means "the joints [rounded contours] of your thighs."
notes.7:4: Latin "filiae multitudinis" ("daughter of the multitude") translates the Hebrew place name Bath-rabbim literally.
notes.7:5: Latin "purpura regis vincta canalibus" ("a king's purple bound in channels") is a distinct Vulgate reading depicting royal purple cloth or yarn fastened in dyeing troughs, where the Hebrew is usually read as a king held captive in the tresses.
notes.7:9: Latin "labiisque et dentibus illius ad ruminandum" ("for his lips and teeth to chew over") is a distinct Vulgate reading; the Hebrew reads of wine gliding over the lips of sleepers.
notes.7:10: Latin "conversio" ("turning") follows the Greek Septuagint ("epistrophe") rather than the Hebrew word for "desire."
notes.7:12: Latin "ubera mea" ("my breasts") follows the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew Masoretic reading "my love."
notes.8:2: Latin "ibi me docebis" ("there you will teach me") takes the Hebrew verb as second-person future and adds ibi ("there"); the Hebrew form can also be read "she will teach me."
notes.8:5: Latin "deliciis affluens" ("overflowing with delights") has no counterpart in the Hebrew Masoretic Text; "corrupta est" ("was corrupted") and "violata est" ("was violated") reflect the other sense ("to corrupt") of the Hebrew root that here means "was in labor."
notes.8:6: Latin "infernus" denotes the underworld or realm of the dead, and "lampades ... ignis atque flammarum" ("torches of fire and of flames") contains no divine name at the end of the verse, whereas the final Hebrew word ends in -yah, which may represent the divine name ("a flame of the Lord") or a superlative ("a mighty flame").
notes.8:7: Latin uses the past tense "non potuerunt" ("could not") and singular "despiciet eam" ("he will despise it," referring to his wealth), whereas the Hebrew uses an impersonal plural.
notes.8:11: Latin renders the Hebrew names Solomon and Baal-hamon etymologically as "pacifico" ("the peaceful one," continued in v. 12 with the Clementine genitive "tui pacifici") and "in ea quae habet populos" ("in that which has peoples").
